learningGoals: Calculate two years of compound growth on a simple amount and see the growth on growth.
Explain why starting early can matter more than starting with a bigger amount.
Name rate and time as the two drivers, and treat any rate shown as an assumption.

keyIdeas.explanation: With compounding, each year's growth is added to the amount, so next year's growth is calculated on a bigger number. ₹1,000 at an assumed 10% becomes ₹1,100, then ₹1,210.
Money left for longer compounds more times. Two savers with the same amount and rate end far apart if one starts years earlier.
A higher rate or a longer time both add growth. Higher possible rates usually come with more risk, and no future rate is guaranteed.

misconceptions.misconception: 10% a year for two years means exactly 20% growth.
misconceptions.correction: With compounding it's more than 20% (21% in this example), because the second year's 10% is on the bigger amount.
Compounding is maths on an assumed rate. Real returns can be lower or even negative, so projections are assumptions, not promises.

misconceptions.misconception: Starting late is fine if you save a bit more.
misconceptions.correction: Saving more helps, but lost years can't be bought back. Time is the hardest thing to make up.

examples: ₹1,000 at an assumed 10% a year: ₹1,100 after one year, ₹1,210 after two, about ₹2,594 after ten.
Asha and Bilal (fictional) save the same amount every month at the same assumed rate; Asha starts five years earlier and ends with noticeably more.

quizObjectives.objective: Compute the value after two years of compound growth on a round amount.
Compare two savers who differ only in start date and pick who ends higher.
Identify rate and time as the drivers, rejecting irrelevant factors.
